title: Hempstead Plains Deed Landscape, 1643
summary: The 1643 Hempstead deed names Masepeage, Merriack, and Rockaway people in an agreement concerning the great plain, woods, and South Shore meadows. Later Native testimony challenged both payment and the authority claimed over this land.
address_label: Hempstead Plains / south side landscape, Town of Hempstead
ancestral_territory_note: Linked to Merrick Ancestral Land as one of the communities named in the Hempstead deed tradition.
why_this_matters: The 1643 Hempstead Plains record is a key entry point into Merrick land loss. It presents dispossession as a legal, ecological, and community transformation across Native homelands.
introduction_title: A Native homeland in the Hempstead agreement
introduction_content: The 1643 Hempstead deed names Masepeage, Merriack, and Rockaway people in an agreement concerning the great plain, woods, and South Shore meadows. Later Native testimony challenged both payment and the authority claimed over this land.12
history_content:
Native homelands before the deed

The great plain met woods, marshes, and coastal meadows used by Native communities. The 1643 agreement names Masepeage, Merriack, and Rockaway and identifies English purchasers Robert Fordham and John Carman. Its surviving signatures and marks preserve multiple Native participants, whose names can be followed in Merrick People in Early Land Records.1

One copy, preserved among Carman family papers and printed by B. Fernow, is dated November 13, 1643. Another deed tradition uses December 13. The document’s language reaches across woods, meadows, marshes, and pasture. It concerns a broad homeland rather than one modern property.13

An agreement followed by disputes

Later conferences and complaints show that the transaction did not end questions of authority or payment. In the Mercock land dispute of August 5, 1675, Native speakers denied that Hempstead had paid for their land and disputed the right of another sachem to convey it. The contrast between the deed and that hearing reveals how sharply colonial claims could diverge from the claims of the people whose homeland was involved.2
